Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Present or describe to an already familiar audience

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) is a rice-cultivation technique in which paddies are intermittently drained rather than continuously flooded.
• Over two growing seasons, agronomists in Bangladesh compared AWD paddies with conventionally flooded paddies.
• The AWD paddies required 28% less irrigation water than the conventional paddies.
• Grain yields from the two kinds of paddies differed by less than 2%, a discrepancy the researchers considered negligible.
• The researchers suggested that AWD could reduce groundwater depletion in rice-producing regions.
items.stem: The student wants to summarize the study’s findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: AWD paddies, the researchers found, needed only 28% as much irrigation water as conventionally flooded paddies, and their yields differed by less than 2%.
Over two growing seasons, agronomists in Bangladesh compared rice paddies that were intermittently drained with paddies that were kept continuously flooded.
The researchers found that AWD paddies used considerably less irrigation water than conventionally flooded paddies while producing nearly the same yields.
The researchers found that AWD paddies used 28% less irrigation water than conventionally flooded paddies and reduced groundwater depletion in rice-producing regions.
items.explanation: The goal is to summarize the findings. The notes report two: the AWD paddies “required 28% less irrigation water than the conventional paddies,” and grain yields “differed by less than 2%, a discrepancy the researchers considered negligible.” Choice C states both findings accurately in its own words: considerably less water, nearly the same yields.

A.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: number misread, 28% less becomes 28% as much)
A.why_wrong: It reports both findings but misstates the first: the AWD paddies “required 28% less irrigation water,” which is not the same as using only 28% as much.

B.why_wrong: It describes how the study was carried out, not what the researchers found.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: suggestion presented as a finding)
D.why_wrong: It reports the water savings correctly, but the study did not find that AWD reduced groundwater depletion; the researchers only “suggested that AWD could reduce groundwater depletion.” It also leaves out the yield finding.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (rice irrigation). Unnamed, generic study; the figures are invented and attached to no identifiable study (WAVE.md wave-3 lesson). Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped (28% less read as 28% as much, as in official 5645f119 D), B true but method only, D FALSE goal-shaped (the suggested groundwater effect stated as a finding). Goal-only solve (no notes): A, C and D all summarize findings.
band7_moves: present-the-findings goal with two numeric findings on different measures
key drops both numbers and states the findings in its own words (considerably less water, nearly the same yields)
FALSE option that misreads the 28% figure (28% less becomes 28% as much) while keeping the yield finding right
FALSE option that states the researchers’ suggestion as a finding

fixes: A rebuilt as a goal-shaped FALSE that reads “28% less” as “28% as much” (official 5645f119 D recipe); the old A was killed by the less-than-2% yield bullet alone
D rebuilt as a goal-shaped FALSE that states the researchers’ groundwater suggestion as a finding; the old D repeated A’s 28%-on-yield move
key wording “far less” changed to “considerably less” (28% is not extreme)
explanation, why_wrong, notes and band7_moves updated

band7.why: Official 5645f119 pattern after hardening: present-the-findings goal with two numeric findings, key drops both numbers, two goal-shaped FALSE options (28% less read as 28% as much; a suggestion stated as a finding), one accurate method option. Goal-only solve leaves A, C and D. Notes 39% words past rank 10,000 (spec at least 14%).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A national anthem is a patriotic song that a country officially adopts as a symbol of its identity.
• South Africa’s anthem, adopted in 1997, incorporates lyrics in five of the eleven official languages the country then recognized.
• Its verses progress from isiXhosa and isiZulu to Sesotho, Afrikaans, and English.
• New Zealand’s anthem, “God Defend New Zealand,” has official lyrics in both English and te reo Māori.
• At international sporting competitions, it is customarily performed first in te reo Māori and then in English.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the languages used in national anthems. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Rather than being limited to a single language, some national anthems combine more than one of the languages spoken in their countries.
Some national anthems combine more than one language, as can be seen in South Africa’s anthem, which is performed entirely in English and Afrikaans.
At international sporting competitions, New Zealand’s anthem is customarily performed first in te reo Māori and then in English.
National anthems typically include lyrics in each of the official languages recognized by the countries that adopt them.
items.explanation: A generalization makes a broad claim about national anthems as a group rather than about one anthem. The notes give two cases: South Africa’s anthem “incorporates lyrics in five of the eleven official languages,” and New Zealand’s “has official lyrics in both English and te reo Māori.” Choice A draws the general point these cases share: some anthems use more than one of their countries’ languages.

B.why_wrong: It makes a general claim, but its support is wrong: South Africa’s anthem moves through five languages, not just English and Afrikaans.

C.why_wrong: It describes how one anthem is performed at sporting competitions; it makes no claim about national anthems in general.

D.why_wrong: It makes a generalization, but the notes contradict it: South Africa’s anthem uses “five of the eleven official languages the country then recognized,” not all of them.

items.notes: Subject: social science and culture (national anthems). Real facts known without a search: South Africa’s 1997 anthem uses isiXhosa, isiZulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans and English (eleven official languages then, twelve since 2023, hence “at the time”); New Zealand’s anthem has official English and Maori lyrics. Option fact check: B FALSE goal-shaped (generalization plus false support), C true single case, D FALSE goal-shaped (overgeneralization: all official languages). Goal-only solve: A, B and D all make a generalization about anthem languages.
band7_moves: generalization climbs from two anthems to anthems as a class
goal-shaped FALSE option: a generalization supported by a misstated case
goal-shaped FALSE option: an overgeneralization (every official language) that the five-of-eleven bullet contradicts

fixes: D rebuilt as a goal-shaped FALSE generalization (anthems use every official language), contradicted by “five of the eleven”; the old D was a contrast, not a generalization, killed by one fact

band7.why: GEN climbs from two anthems to anthems as a class; two goal-shaped FALSE options (a generalization with misstated support; an overgeneralization the five-of-eleven bullet contradicts) and one true single case, as 7f5715e4 and 3b02e88a. Goal-only solve leaves A, B and D. Notes 30% rare words.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the fire-prone shrublands of southwestern Australia, many plant species have ways to persist after fire.
• Resprouters survive fire, producing new shoots from dormant buds protected beneath thick bark or inside woody swellings at the base of the stem.
• These swellings, called lignotubers, also store carbohydrates that fuel regrowth.
• Obligate seeders are killed by fire.
• Their populations regenerate from seeds stored in the soil or in woody fruits that open only after burning.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in how the two kinds of plants recover after a fire. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Resprouters and obligate seeders both have strategies that allow their species to persist in fire-prone shrublands.
Resprouters store their seeds in carbohydrate-rich lignotubers, whereas obligate seeders store theirs in the soil or in woody fruits.
Obligate seeders are killed by fire, but their populations regenerate from seeds stored in the soil or in woody fruits.
While resprouters regrow from buds that survive a fire, obligate seeders die and are replaced by new plants grown from seed.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast how the two kinds of plants recover. According to the notes, resprouters produce “new shoots from dormant buds protected beneath thick bark or inside woody swellings,” while obligate seeders “are killed by fire” and their populations regenerate “from seeds stored in the soil or in woody fruits.” Choice D states both sides of that contrast.

A.why_wrong: It states what the two kinds of plants have in common, not how they differ.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: wrong storage attached to resprouters)
B.why_wrong: It offers a contrast, but the notes say lignotubers hold dormant buds and carbohydrates, not seeds; resprouters regrow from buds.

C.why_wrong: It describes only how obligate seeders recover and says nothing about resprouters, so there is no contrast.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (fire ecology, resprouters and obligate seeders in southwestern Australia). Real ecology known without a search; no named people. Hard cell with band_target 6 (plan). Option fact check: A true similarity, B FALSE goal-shaped contrast (seeds put in lignotubers), C true one side.

band7.why: Planned band 6: one goal-shaped FALSE contrast (seeds put in lignotubers), one similarity and one side only; the compared dimension is the stated one, so it is a fair band 6, not 7.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Zuiderzee was a shallow inlet of the North Sea whose storm surges repeatedly flooded communities in the central Netherlands.
• In 1891, civil engineer Cornelis Lely devised a plan to enclose the inlet with a long dam.
• As minister of public works, Lely later secured passage of a 1918 law authorizing the project.
• Lely died in 1929, three years before construction of the 32-kilometer dam, the Afsluitdijk, was completed.
• Behind the dam, the enclosed inlet gradually became a freshwater lake, the IJsselmeer.
items.stem: The student wants to identify Lely’s role in the closing of the Zuiderzee. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Storm surges from the Zuiderzee, a shallow inlet of the North Sea, repeatedly flooded communities in the central Netherlands.
Lely devised the plan to dam the Zuiderzee and later secured passage of the 1918 law that authorized the project.
Cornelis Lely oversaw construction of the 32-kilometer Afsluitdijk until its completion in 1932.
After it was completed in 1932, the Afsluitdijk gradually turned the Zuiderzee into a freshwater lake, the IJsselmeer.
items.explanation: The goal is to identify what Lely did. The notes say that “In 1891, civil engineer Cornelis Lely devised a plan to enclose the inlet with a long dam” and that he “later secured passage of a 1918 law authorizing the project.” Choice B states both of these contributions.

A.recipe: OG (background: why the inlet was closed)
A.why_wrong: It explains the problem the dam addressed but says nothing about what Lely did.

C.why_wrong: The notes never say Lely oversaw construction, and he could not have seen it through to completion: he “died in 1929, three years before construction of the 32-kilometer dam, the Afsluitdijk, was completed.”

D.why_wrong: It describes what the dam did to the inlet, not Lely’s role in the project.

items.notes: Subject: history (Zuiderzee Works, Netherlands). Real facts known without a search: Lely’s 1891 plan, the 1918 Zuiderzee Act passed while he was minister of Waterstaat, his death in January 1929, the Afsluitdijk closed in 1932, about 32 km, the IJsselmeer. Plan cell was band_target 7, but SPEC has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md), so it is written as a strong band 6 on the 3.19 model (a misattribution FALSE option beside two accurate off-goal options).

fixes: C made plainly false (“oversaw construction ... until its completion in 1932”; Lely died in 1929); why_wrong logic fixed, since dying before completion did not by itself rule out overseeing part of the work

band7.why: SPEC has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md), so band 7 is out of reach; strong band 6 on the 3.19 model: a misattribution FALSE option beside two accurate off-goal options.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Nations apply different legal principles when determining citizenship at birth.
• Under jus soli (Latin for “right of the soil”), a child born within a country’s territory automatically becomes a citizen of that country.
• The United States, Canada, and Brazil follow this principle.
• Under jus sanguinis (“right of blood”), a child’s citizenship is determined by the citizenship of the child’s parents, regardless of birthplace.
• Japan and Italy follow this principle.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between jus soli and jus sanguinis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Whereas jus soli bases a child’s citizenship on where the child is born, jus sanguinis bases it on the parents’ citizenship.
Jus soli and jus sanguinis are two distinct legal principles that countries follow when granting citizenship.
In the United States, Canada, and Brazil, children born within the country’s territory automatically become citizens.
Both jus soli and jus sanguinis determine whether a child receives a country’s citizenship at birth.
items.explanation: Choice A contrasts the two principles on the same point. Under jus soli, “a child born within a country’s territory automatically becomes a citizen,” while under jus sanguinis, citizenship “is determined by the citizenship of the child’s parents, regardless of birthplace.”

B.why_wrong: It says the principles are distinct but never says how they differ.

C.why_wrong: It describes only how jus soli works in three countries and says nothing about jus sanguinis.

D.why_wrong: It states what the two principles have in common, not how they differ.

items.notes: Subject: social science (citizenship law). Real, well-established facts known without a search (United States, Canada and Brazil grant unconditional birthright citizenship; Japan and Italy follow descent).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Repoussé and chasing are two techniques for decorating sheet metal.
• In both, the metalworker shapes the metal with hammers and blunt punches instead of cutting it.
• In repoussé, the metal is hammered from the back, so the design bulges outward on the front.
• In chasing, the metal is worked from the front, pressing outlines and intricate details into the surface.
• Artisans frequently combine the two techniques on a single decorative object.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how the metal is worked in repoussé and in chasing. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In both repoussé and chasing, the metalworker uses hammers and blunt punches to shape the metal instead of cutting it.
In repoussé, the metal is hammered from the back so that the design bulges outward on the front.
In repoussé, the metal is hammered from the back, while in chasing, it is worked from the front.
Repoussé and chasing, which artisans frequently combine, differ in how the metalworker approaches the sheet metal.
items.explanation: Choice C contrasts the two techniques on the point the goal names, how the metal is worked: in repoussé “the metal is hammered from the back,” while in chasing “the metal is worked from the front.”

A.why_wrong: It states what the two techniques share rather than how they differ.

B.why_wrong: It describes repoussé alone and says nothing about chasing.

D.why_wrong: It says the techniques differ in how the metal is approached but never says what the difference is.

items.notes: Subject: arts (metalworking techniques). Real, standard definitions known without a search; no named people.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sand dunes cover only a portion of the Sahara.
• An erg is a broad expanse of desert covered by windblown sand, often shaped into dunes.
• Ergs constitute roughly a quarter of the Sahara’s total area.
• A reg is a flat desert plain covered with tightly packed gravel and pebbles.
• Regs develop where wind gradually removes the finer sand, leaving heavier stones behind.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between ergs and regs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Sand dunes cover only a portion of the Sahara, with ergs making up roughly a quarter of the desert.
Unlike an erg, which is covered by windblown sand, a reg is a flat plain of tightly packed stones.
Both ergs and regs are desert landscapes shaped by the wind, which either deposits sand or gradually removes it.
Regs develop where the wind gradually removes the finer sand, leaving the heavier stones behind.
items.explanation: Choice B contrasts the surfaces of the two landscapes: an erg is “covered by windblown sand,” whereas a reg is “a flat desert plain covered with tightly packed gravel and pebbles.”

A.recipe: OG (how much of the Sahara is sand)
A.why_wrong: It gives the share of the Sahara covered by ergs but says nothing about regs.

C.why_wrong: It states a way the two landscapes are alike, not how they differ.

D.why_wrong: It explains how regs develop without contrasting them with ergs.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (desert geomorphology). Real terms and figures known without a search (ergs are commonly put at about a fifth to a quarter of the Sahara).

items.subtype: Introduce a term to a new audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the decades before printed billboards became widespread, many businesses hired sign painters to paint advertisements directly onto brick walls.
• Some of these hand-painted ads from the late 1800s and early 1900s are still faintly visible today.
• These faded advertisements are known as ghost signs.
• Many were painted with lead-based paint, which bonded with the brick and helped the signs endure.
• Some municipalities now photograph and document their ghost signs before they disappear.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce ghost signs to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Because they were painted with lead-based paint that bonded with the brick, many ghost signs have endured for over a century.
Before printed billboards became widespread, businesses often hired sign painters to advertise directly on brick walls.
Some municipalities now photograph and document their ghost signs so that a record of them survives after the signs disappear.
Ghost signs are faded advertisements, hand-painted on brick walls in the late 1800s and early 1900s, that remain faintly visible.
items.explanation: An audience unfamiliar with ghost signs needs to learn what they are. Choice D explains that they are “faded advertisements,” hand-painted “directly onto brick walls” in “the late 1800s and early 1900s,” that “are still faintly visible today.”

A.why_wrong: It explains why ghost signs last but assumes the reader already knows what a ghost sign is.

B.why_wrong: It describes how businesses once advertised but never mentions ghost signs.

C.why_wrong: It describes what some municipalities do with ghost signs without saying what ghost signs are.

items.notes: Subject: arts and social history (ghost signs). Real phenomenon known without a search; no named people or places.

items.subtype: Describe a technique to an audience new to it
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Joyce J. Scott is an American artist based in Baltimore, Maryland.
• She is best known for sculptures and jewelry made of thousands of small glass beads.
• She joins the beads using the peyote stitch.
• The peyote stitch is a method of weaving beads together with a needle and thread, without a loom.
• Her mother, Elizabeth Talford Scott, was a noted quilter.
• In 2016, Scott received a MacArthur Fellowship.
items.stem: The student wants to describe how Scott makes her sculptures to an audience unfamiliar with the peyote stitch. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Scott’s sculptures are made of glass beads joined by the peyote stitch, a way of weaving beads with a needle and thread rather than a loom.
Scott joins the thousands of small glass beads in her sculptures and jewelry using the peyote stitch.
Baltimore artist Joyce J. Scott, whose mother, Elizabeth Talford Scott, was a noted quilter, received a prestigious MacArthur Fellowship in 2016.
The peyote stitch is a method of weaving beads together with a needle and thread rather than on a loom.
items.explanation: Readers unfamiliar with the peyote stitch need it explained. Choice A says Scott’s sculptures are made of “thousands of small glass beads” joined by the peyote stitch and explains that the stitch is “a method of weaving beads together with a needle and thread, without a loom.”

B.why_wrong: It names the peyote stitch but does not explain it, so readers new to the stitch would not understand how Scott works.

C.why_wrong: It gives facts about Scott’s family and an award but says nothing about how she makes her sculptures.

D.why_wrong: It explains the stitch but never connects it to Scott or her sculptures.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Joyce J. Scott, Baltimore beadwork artist). Thin real facts held firmly without a search: Baltimore, beaded sculpture and jewelry, peyote stitch (off-loom bead weaving), mother Elizabeth Talford Scott a quilter, MacArthur Fellowship 2016.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Sanborn Map Company, founded in 1867, produced detailed maps for fire insurance companies.
• The maps showed each building’s outline, height, and construction material, with brick in pink and wood in yellow.
• Insurers used them to estimate each building’s vulnerability to fire.
• Over about a century, the company mapped some 12,000 cities and towns across the United States.
• Historians now use the maps to trace how neighborhoods changed.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how extensive the Sanborn Map Company’s coverage of the United States was. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Sanborn maps used colors to show construction materials, marking brick buildings in pink and wooden ones in yellow.
Over about a century, the Sanborn Map Company’s maps came to cover some 12,000 cities and towns across the United States.
Historians now use maps made by the Sanborn Map Company, which was founded in 1867, to trace how city neighborhoods changed over time.
The Sanborn Map Company made detailed maps that fire insurance companies used to estimate each building’s vulnerability to fire.
items.explanation: The goal is to stress how much of the country the company covered. Choice B does this with the number in the notes: “some 12,000 cities and towns across the United States.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the maps’ color code, not how many places they covered.

C.why_wrong: It explains how historians use the maps today without saying how many places were mapped.

D.why_wrong: It explains what the maps were for, not how extensive the coverage was.

items.notes: Subject: history (Sanborn fire insurance maps). Real facts known without a search: founded 1867 by D. A. Sanborn, color code (pink brick, yellow frame), about 12,000 US cities and towns in the Library of Congress set.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The shepherd’s tree (Boscia albitrunca) grows in dry savannas of southern Africa, including the Kalahari.
• It is an evergreen with a pale trunk and rarely grows taller than 10 meters.
• In the Kalahari, its roots have been found about 68 meters below the surface.
• That is one of the deepest root systems recorded for any plant.
• Livestock browse its foliage during droughts, when other vegetation is scarce.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how deep the shepherd’s tree’s roots can reach. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: An evergreen with a pale trunk, the shepherd’s tree grows in the dry savannas of southern Africa.
During droughts, when other vegetation is scarce, livestock in southern Africa browse the foliage of the shepherd’s tree.
The shepherd’s tree’s roots have been found 68 meters underground, among the deepest recorded for any plant.
The shepherd’s tree, which rarely grows taller than 10 meters, has roots that extend below the surface of the Kalahari.
items.explanation: Choice C stresses the depth of the roots with both the figure and its rank: roots “about 68 meters below the surface,” “one of the deepest root systems recorded for any plant.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the tree and where it grows, not its roots.

B.why_wrong: It explains how livestock use the tree’s foliage, not how deep its roots reach.

D.why_wrong: It says the roots extend below the surface but gives no sense of how far, so it does not emphasize their depth.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany, Kalahari). Real figure known without a search: Boscia albitrunca roots recorded at 68 m, often cited as the deepest known.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Nacreous clouds are rare, brightly colored clouds named for nacre, the shimmering material that lines some seashells.
• They form in the stratosphere, about 15 to 25 kilometers above the ground.
• Because the air there is extremely dry, clouds can form only when temperatures drop below about −78°C.
• The stratosphere reaches such temperatures mainly over polar regions in winter.
• The clouds are most visible shortly before sunrise or after sunset.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why nacreous clouds are usually seen only over polar regions in winter. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Named for the shimmering material that lines some seashells, nacreous clouds are most visible shortly before sunrise or after sunset.
Nacreous clouds form in the stratosphere, about 15 to 25 kilometers above the ground, where the air is extremely dry.
Nacreous clouds appear over polar regions in winter because conditions there suit their formation.
Nacreous clouds can form only when the dry stratosphere drops below about −78°C, which happens mainly over polar regions in winter.
items.explanation: Choice D links the effect to its cause. In the dry stratosphere, “clouds can form only when temperatures drop below about −78°C,” and the stratosphere “reaches such temperatures mainly over polar regions in winter.”

A.why_wrong: It gives the origin of the name and the best time of day to see the clouds, not why they appear only over polar regions in winter.

B.why_wrong: It says where the clouds form but leaves out the temperature condition that limits them to polar winters.

C.why_wrong: It says conditions there suit the clouds without saying what those conditions are.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (atmosphere). Real facts known without a search: nacreous (polar stratospheric) clouds form about 15 to 25 km up below about −78°C, mainly in polar winter.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Traditional Mongolian script was adapted from the Old Uyghur alphabet in the early 1200s.
• It is written in vertical columns, read from top to bottom, with successive columns proceeding from left to right.
• Japanese can also be written vertically, an arrangement known as tategaki.
• In tategaki, characters run from top to bottom in columns that proceed from right to left.
• Many Japanese novels and newspapers are still published in tategaki.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between traditional Mongolian script and Japanese tategaki. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Columns of traditional Mongolian script proceed from left to right, whereas columns of tategaki proceed from right to left.
In both traditional Mongolian script and Japanese tategaki, text is written in vertical columns that read from top to bottom.
Adapted from the Old Uyghur alphabet in the early 1200s, traditional Mongolian script is written in vertical columns.
Many Japanese novels and newspapers are still published in tategaki, with characters running from top to bottom.
items.explanation: Choice B names both writing systems and the trait they share: Mongolian script “is written in vertical columns, read from top to bottom,” and in tategaki “characters run from top to bottom in columns.”

A.why_wrong: It contrasts the direction in which the columns proceed, a difference rather than a similarity.

C.why_wrong: It describes only Mongolian script and never mentions tategaki.

D.why_wrong: It describes only tategaki and never mentions Mongolian script.

items.notes: Subject: social science (writing systems). Real facts known without a search: traditional Mongolian script, from Old Uyghur in the early 1200s, written top to bottom in columns running left to right; Japanese tategaki runs top to bottom in columns from right to left.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mammoth Cave, in Kentucky, is the longest known cave system in the world.
• Explorers have surveyed more than 670 kilometers of its interconnected passages.
• Sistema Sac Actun, on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, is the longest known underwater cave system.
• Divers have mapped about 370 kilometers of its flooded passages.
• Both caves formed as slightly acidic water gradually dissolved limestone.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how the mapped length of Sistema Sac Actun compares with that of Mammoth Cave. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Though it is the longest known underwater cave system, Sistema Sac Actun has only about half the mapped length of Mammoth Cave.
Explorers have mapped more than 670 kilometers of Mammoth Cave, and divers have mapped about 370 kilometers of Sistema Sac Actun.
Both Mammoth Cave and Sistema Sac Actun formed as slightly acidic water gradually dissolved limestone.
On Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, Sistema Sac Actun is the longest known underwater cave system in the world.
items.explanation: The goal asks how one length compares with the other. The notes give “about 370 kilometers” for Sistema Sac Actun and “more than 670 kilometers” for Mammoth Cave; Choice A states the relation, that Sac Actun’s mapped length is only about half of Mammoth Cave’s.

B.why_wrong: It gives both lengths but never states how they compare.

C.why_wrong: It states how both caves formed, not how their lengths compare.

D.why_wrong: It describes Sistema Sac Actun’s rank among underwater caves without comparing it with Mammoth Cave.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (caves). Real figures, rounded, known without a search: Mammoth Cave over 420 miles (about 680 km) surveyed; Sistema Sac Actun about 370 km. 370/670 = 0.55 or less, so “about half” holds.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Children on isolated cattle stations in central Australia once lived hundreds of kilometers from the nearest school.
• In 1951, the Alice Springs School of the Air began broadcasting lessons to these children.
• Students and teachers communicated through two-way radios.
• The radios belonged to the network of the Royal Flying Doctor Service, which used it to reach isolated patients.
• Today, the school instructs its students through satellite internet connections.
items.stem: The student wants to specify the technology that students first used to take part in the school’s lessons. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Children on isolated cattle stations in central Australia once lived hundreds of kilometers from the nearest school.
Students of the Alice Springs School of the Air take part in lessons through satellite internet connections.
When the Alice Springs School of the Air opened in 1951, students took part in lessons through two-way radios.
The Royal Flying Doctor Service used its radio network to reach isolated patients in central Australia.
items.explanation: The goal asks for the technology students first used. The notes say the school began in 1951 and that “Students and teachers communicated through two-way radios,” which Choice C specifies.

items.notes: Subject: history (Alice Springs School of the Air, 1951, radio lessons over the Royal Flying Doctor Service network). Real facts known without a search; “hundreds of kilometers” is a plain description of the distances, not a figure.

items.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of an eponym. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

An eponym is a word that is derived from the name of an individual.
The snug, one-piece garments known as leotards are named after the French acrobat Jules Léotard.
An eponym is a word derived from a person’s name; “leotard,” for example, comes from the French acrobat Jules Léotard.
items.explanation: Choice D gives both parts of the goal: the explanation, that eponyms are “words derived from the names of individuals,” and an example, “leotard,” which comes from the name of the acrobat Jules Léotard.

items.notes: Subject: social science (language, eponyms). Real facts known without a search: Jules Léotard, French acrobat, flying trapeze act in Paris in 1859, the garment named for him, and George Leybourne’s 1867 song inspired by him.

items.subtype: Present the study and its findings
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Researchers in Brazil strung rope bridges between trees on opposite sides of a forest road.
• They wanted to determine whether arboreal mammals would use the bridges rather than descend and cross on the ground.
• Motion-activated cameras monitored the bridges continuously for two years.
• Six mammal species, including two kinds of monkeys, crossed the bridges more than 1,000 times.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After stringing rope bridges over a forest road in Brazil, researchers recorded six mammal species, including two kinds of monkeys, crossing them more than 1,000 times.
Six mammal species, including two kinds of monkeys, crossed rope bridges more than 1,000 times.
Researchers in Brazil wanted to determine whether arboreal mammals would cross a forest road on rope bridges rather than on the ground.
Researchers used motion-activated cameras to monitor rope bridges strung between trees on opposite sides of a forest road in Brazil.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: the study and what it found. Choice A presents the study (researchers “strung rope bridges between trees on opposite sides of a forest road” in Brazil) and its finding (“Six mammal species, including two kinds of monkeys, crossed the bridges more than 1,000 times”).

B.why_wrong: It gives the result but does not present the study that produced it.

C.why_wrong: It states what the researchers wanted to learn, not what they found.

D.why_wrong: It describes how the bridges were monitored but gives no findings.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (wildlife crossings). Unnamed, generic study; the species count, crossings and duration are invented and attached to no identifiable study (WAVE.md wave-3 lesson).

items.subtype: Describe a work to an audience familiar with the artist
items.passage:

• Her painting Trade (Gifts for Trading Land with White People) dates from 1992, the 500th anniversary of Columbus’s first voyage.

• Above it hangs a chain of objects, such as toy tomahawks and sports souvenirs bearing Native American mascots.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Trade to an audience already familiar with Quick-to-See Smith. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, a painter and printmaker who was an enrolled Salish and Kootenai citizen, created Trade in 1992.
Quick-to-See Smith’s 1992 painting Trade combines paint with collaged newspaper clippings beneath a hanging chain of objects such as toy tomahawks.
The subject of a 2023 retrospective at New York’s Whitney Museum, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith was an enrolled Salish and Kootenai citizen.
Quick-to-See Smith, an enrolled Salish and Kootenai citizen, combined paint with collaged newspaper clippings in her 1992 painting Trade.
items.explanation: An audience that already knows the artist needs a description of the work, not of her. Choice B describes Trade itself: a canvas that “combines paint with collaged newspaper clippings” with “a chain of objects, such as toy tomahawks,” hanging above it.

A.why_wrong: It spends its words introducing Quick-to-See Smith, whom the audience already knows, and never describes what Trade looks like.

C.why_wrong: It describes the artist and an exhibition of her work, not the painting Trade.

D.why_wrong: It spends words introducing Quick-to-See Smith, whom the audience already knows, and it leaves out the chain of objects that hangs above the canvas.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, Trade (Gifts for Trading Land with White People), 1992, Chrysler Museum of Art). Thin real facts held firmly without a search: Salish and Kootenai citizen, 2023 Whitney retrospective Memory Map, Trade made for the 1992 Columbus quincentenary, collaged canvas with a chain of souvenirs (toy tomahawks, sports items with Native mascots) hung above. Review: Smith died in January 2025 (Wikipedia), so the notes and options use the past tense for her.

fixes: Quick-to-See Smith died in January 2025 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaune_Quick-to-See_Smith, fetched): notes and options A and C put in the past tense
D replaced: the old D (1992, the Columbus quincentenary) was weakly defensible as describing Trade; the new D re-introduces the artist and gives only part of the description (AUD)

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Harris Tweed is a wool cloth that, by law, must be handwoven by islanders at their homes in Scotland’s Outer Hebrides.
• Seonag Macaulay has woven it in a workshop beside her house on the Isle of Lewis for over three decades.
• She blends dyed wools to echo the surrounding landscape.
• She says, “Every tweed I make is a piece of the hillside: purple heather and brown bracken mixed through the green.”
• Of her working days, she says, “Most days it is just me, the loom, and the radio.”
items.stem: The student wants to provide a quotation from Macaulay that explains how the landscape shapes her tweeds. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Macaulay blends dyed wools so that the colors of her tweeds echo the landscape surrounding her home on the Isle of Lewis.
Describing her working days, Macaulay says that “most days it is just me, the loom, and the radio.”
Macaulay blends dyed wools to echo the landscape, calling each tweed “a piece of the hillside: purple heather and brown bracken mixed through the green.”
By law, Harris Tweed must be handwoven by islanders such as Macaulay at their homes in the Outer Hebrides.
items.explanation: The goal calls for a quotation that explains how the landscape shapes Macaulay’s cloth. Choice C quotes her description of each tweed as “a piece of the hillside: purple heather and brown bracken mixed through the green,” which shows the hillside’s colors in the wool.

A.why_wrong: It explains the link to the landscape but uses no quotation from Macaulay.

B.why_wrong: It quotes Macaulay, but the quotation describes her solitary working days, not how the landscape shapes her tweeds.

D.why_wrong: It states the law about where Harris Tweed is woven and contains no quotation.

items.notes: Subject: arts and crafts (Harris Tweed, Outer Hebrides; real legal requirement under the Harris Tweed Act 1993). Seonag Macaulay is an invented weaver and her words are invented; one web search for the name found no such person (other Macaulays appear in island weaving records, none with this first name).

fixes: notes and D: “in their own homes” changed to “at their homes” (the Harris Tweed Act wording, consistent with her workshop beside the house)

items.stem: The student wants to identify which of the three mountains is the highest. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya, and Mount Stanley all have glaciers that persist on portions of their summits.
At 5,895 meters, Mount Kilimanjaro is higher than both Mount Kenya and Mount Stanley.
Mount Stanley is located in the Rwenzori Mountains on Uganda’s western border.
items.explanation: Choice C identifies the highest mountain and compares it with the other two: at “5,895 meters,” Kilimanjaro rises higher than Mount Kenya (“5,199 meters”) and Mount Stanley (“5,109 meters”).

items.notes: Subject: geography (East African peaks). Real heights known without a search. Mount Stanley added to the claimed pair (Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya) as the third peak.
